title: Moved instead of stopped
roles: Sent abusers away and received them
summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

facts.t: Pennsylvania grand jury — six dioceses: A 23-member statewide grand jury report released by Attorney General Josh Shapiro on 14 August 2018 identified 301 'predator priests' and at least 1,000 child victims over about 70 years in six dioceses. The roughly 1,400-page report found bishops 'went to great lengths to keep it secret' and moved abusers. Most crimes were too old to prosecute.

Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.

John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review): A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

University of Zurich pilot study (Dommann and Meier), commissioned by Swiss Bishops' Conference, RKZ and KOVOS; report May/Sept 2023: 1,002 cases, 510 accused, 921 victims; superiors systematically transferred accused clerics, sometimes abroad, to avoid prosecution

uncertain: The moves drawn are only those a source documents; most church and school personnel files were never opened, and Poland's state commission reported in 2022 that files sent to the Vatican were out of its reach. A move is drawn from where the abuser was sent from to where they went; whether the receiving diocese or country was told is often not recorded.
implications:
Moving an abuser kept the matter inside the institution. No police report was made where the abuse had happened, and the people at the new posting were not told. The receiving places were often poorer or more remote than the sending ones, such as missions in Africa, the Pacific and Latin America and Indigenous communities in northern Canada, where a complaint against a foreign priest was less likely to reach a court.

The records show the same practice in Catholic dioceses and religious orders, in Anglican and evangelical circles, in an ultra-Orthodox Jewish school and in a Scottish private school, over several decades. It went on for as long as these institutions dealt with complaints themselves, and it came to light mainly when grand juries, royal commissions and courts obtained their files.

title: Years of waiting: protected by status
summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

countries.note: Jeffrey Epstein: first report 1996, first action 2006 (10 years). Maria Farmer reported to the FBI in 1996 with no known action; after the 2005 Palm Beach police probe, the 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement ended the federal case and he served 13 months in a county stockade on a state plea (2008). Federal sex-trafficking charges came only in July 2019 after the Miami Herald series (2018) Larry Nassar: first report 1997, first action 2016 (19 years). A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted; a 2001 eyewitness report by Mike McQueary went to Paterno and university leaders, who did not report to police (Freeh report, 2012) Theodore McCarrick: first report 1994, first action 2018 (24 years). A priest wrote to Bishop Hughes in 1994; the nuncio was warned in 1994; further warnings including to Benedict XVI (2008); McCarrick denied them to the Vatican and was made a cardinal in 2001 R. Kelly: first report 2000, first action 2019 (19 years). Chicago Sun-Times investigated from August 2000; 2002 child-pornography prosecution ended in acquittal in 2008 Mark Foley (House pages): first report 2000, first action 2006 (6 years). Allegations surfaced 2007; a franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 Fr Gilbert Gauthe (Lafayette): first report 1974, first action 1985 (11 years). The 1982 Ruston Report described the beatings; the Makin Review (2024) found a cover-up by "powerful evangelical clergy"; Archbishop Justin Welby, told in 2013, took no action and resigned 12 Nov 2024 Fr Brendan Smyth (Norbertines): first report 1975, first action 1991 (16 years). Two people included were acquitted (George Pell, Bishop Franco Mulakkal); their rows record the time to charge, not a finding of guilt.
implications:
A long gap between a complaint and any action means that someone with the power to act knew and did not. The reasons recorded in these cases are of a few kinds. Prosecutors made lenient deals, as with Jeffrey Epstein's non-prosecution agreement in Florida in 2007. Police chiefs closed inquiries, as in St John's, Newfoundland, where an investigation into the Mount Cashel orphanage was shut nine days after it opened in 1975. Complaints were set aside because of who the accused was, as with Cyril Smith. Witnesses were attacked or killed, as in the cases against Asaram Bapu in India and Timothy Omotoso in South Africa. A 1999 magazine investigation into the Japanese talent agent Johnny Kitagawa was upheld in court, but no inquiry followed until 2023.

In several cases nothing happened until the accused had died. When a powerful person is charged after many years, the earlier complaints are usually on record somewhere, together with the names of the people who received them.

title: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
roles: Lobbying against reform and bankruptcy filings
summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

title: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

title: States that shielded their own
summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

The Holy See has said it acts through its own tribunal; its refusal to share files with the Irish and English inquiries is documented, its reasons are its own.
implications:
Diplomatic immunity, extradition rules and military jurisdiction exist to protect a country's officials and soldiers from unfair prosecution abroad. In these cases the same rules protected people accused of abusing children. The children were usually in the poorer of the two countries, such as Haiti, the Central African Republic and the Dominican Republic.

The bodies involved include the United Nations, the Holy See, a South Korean court and an Israeli minister. When a case was referred to the accused person's home country, the records show it usually ended there. The one waiver in these records came in 2019, when the Holy See lifted the immunity of its ambassador in France, who was accused of sexually assaulting adults, after French requests.

title: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
roles: Sending country, later closed or suspended
summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

facts.t: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents.

Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007): After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way.

Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights.

Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank.

China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions): Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

uncertain: Totals are adoptions reported by 23–25 receiving states (Peter Selman's tables) and miss countries that do not report; South Korea's total differs by source (163,898 per its ministry for 1953–2008; up to about 200,000 in AP reporting). A closure means the sending or receiving government stopped or suspended adoptions; the reason given was not always fraud.
implications:
The parents adopting lived mainly in a small number of wealthy countries, including the United States, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the Nordic countries. The children came from countries where families were poor and records of births and guardianship were easy to alter. The fees paid for each child gave intermediaries a reason to find children and to produce the papers that made them available for adoption. The yearly figures show the totals moving from one sending country to the next as each was closed.

In some cases officials knew. South Korea's commission found the state responsible, and the Dutch government said in 2021 that its officials had been aware of wrongdoing for years without intervening. A child could be adopted through a lawful court process while the documents describing that child as an orphan were false.

title: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
roles: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused

summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

facts.t: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict): On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress).

Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher.

British child migration programmes — IICSA: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse.

South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases.

Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987.

uncertain: Numbers of children taken are estimates in most of these cases and differ by source. Removals by governments where the records show no sexual abuse and no false identity or sale (for example Australia's Stolen Generations, Canada's Sixties Scoop, Denmark's 1951 Greenland experiment and Russia's deportation of Ukrainian children) are not on this map, because it covers abuse and trafficking. Spain's courts have convicted nobody for the stolen babies; the one doctor tried (2018) was acquitted on the statute of limitations.
implications:
In these cases the people who took the children worked for the state or under contract to it, so the officials who would normally investigate were part of the same system. Investigation came only after a change of government, as in Argentina after 1983, or when a later inquiry was set up, as in Canada, Britain, Ireland and South Korea.

For many of the people taken as children, the harm continues today. Some still do not know who their parents are, and in Spain and Chile no one has been convicted.

title: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
roles: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

implications:

The UN cannot prosecute peacekeepers. It can send them home, and only their own government can try them, which the records show rarely happened. The yearly numbers of allegations rise and fall with new missions and have not fallen steadily.

Several of the cases that became public, including the trafficking of women and girls in Bosnia around 2001 and the abuse of children in the Central African Republic in 2014 and 2015, came to light through staff who passed information outside their organisation, not through the UN's own reporting.

A few commanders have since been convicted at the International Criminal Court, years later. Most of the children taken were never found, and many were never counted.

title: When spies, soldiers and police are named
roles: Proven link to a state service

summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

facts.t: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them.

Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days: After seizing the server the FBI kept Playpen running from 19 February to 4 March 2015 under a court warrant and used malware (a 'Network Investigative Technique') to unmask users; the EFF criticised the operation as continued distribution, and the 11th Circuit (2019) held the warrant invalid but did not exclude the evidence (good-faith exception).

Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity: Abuse allegations reached the RUC by 1977 without prosecution until 1980; the Hart inquiry found a 'catalogue of failures' by police and authorities. Former army officers Colin Wallace and Brian Gemmell said in 2014 that superiors stopped them passing on or pursuing information.

Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services: In July 2019 journalist Vicky Ward (Daily Beast) reported that Alexander Acosta had told Trump transition interviewers he was told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone; the source was not named.

uncertain: The proven cases show state services that used, tolerated or failed to stop abuse; none shows an intelligence service running a child-abuse network as policy. Individual accounts about Kincora and Epstein remain unresolved, and new document releases may change what is known.
implications:
In the documented cases the state did not set up the abuse. It used it, tolerated it or failed to stop it because something else mattered more to it: a dictatorship's use of a compound, a military alliance, an official theory about foster care, or the chance to identify more offenders online.

The claims that have not held up rest mainly on single witnesses or anonymous sources. When such a claim collapses, as Operation Midland did, later allegations against powerful people become harder to have taken seriously. The difference between the two kinds is whether a court, an inquiry or the agency's own records established the facts.

summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

uncertain: Hosting shares measure where servers are, which can change with one large site; the IWF noted Bulgaria's 2025 jump came from a few sites. CyberTipline country counts reflect where people use US platforms, not where most abuse happens.
implications:
Each stage of online abuse passes through a company that could detect it: the host, the platform, the payment service and the bank. In these records the companies acted mostly after pressure from outside, such as a sheriff's letters to Visa and Mastercard about Backpage in 2015, a newspaper column about Pornhub in 2020 and a regulator's case against Westpac. Changes made for other reasons, such as encrypting messages, have reduced the reports that police rely on.

The child, the viewer and the server are often in three different countries, but the payments and data that connect them pass through regulated businesses, which governments can require to check.

facts.t: Rotherham — Jay inquiry (1,400 children, 1997–2013): Three earlier reports (2002, 2003, 2013) on exploitation were effectively suppressed or ignored; police did not treat the abuse as a priority.

Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care': The earlier Jillings report (commissioned 1994, completed 1996) was shelved and only released in redacted form in 2012 after a BBC Freedom of Information request. North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers rather than having them independently investigated.

Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.

Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.

uncertain: This counts cases whose sources document official involvement or obstruction; it does not measure how common that is in each country, and countries with more inquiries will show more.
implications:
In these records officials rarely set out to help abusers. More often they put another interest first: a council worried about its reputation, a police force protecting its own officers, a politician protecting an ally or a donor. The decision to set a child's complaint aside was made by different people in different places, and in many cases more than once.

Where officials were involved, the abuse usually came to light through someone outside the chain of authority, such as a journalist, a researcher, a court, or an inquiry with the power to demand documents.

title: Where nobody is counting
roles: No survey data on online abuse in its region
No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
Almost no reports reach the international systems
summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

uncertain: The regional groupings follow UNICEF's regions, which Childlight uses; individual countries within a region may have national studies that were not pooled. "No national inquiry found" for Brazil, the Philippines and India is an absence in the sources reached, not a sourced statement.
implications:
A country with few recorded cases may be a country where no one has asked. The places least covered by surveys, official statistics and online reports overlap with places where many children live in poverty, and in some of them the institutions that would be investigated also hold the records.

For this reason the map's country score uses estimates of the trafficking trade and of how much stands in its way, which cover nearly every country, and not the number of cases found.

title: False alarms that drown real cases
summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

uncertain: Operation Underground Railroad and the "Sound of Freedom" story are contested; this map records only what investigations established. A claim being unproven does not make it false; it means no court or inquiry has established it.
implications:
False claims about secret rings of powerful people do two kinds of harm. They use up police and hotline time that could have gone to children in danger, and after they collapse, real allegations against powerful people are more easily dismissed.

The real cases on this map involving politicians, celebrities and bishops were established slowly, through police investigations, courts and inquiries. The viral claims did not go through that process, and none of those listed here led to a child being found or protected.
